chunks.heading: What differentiation studies
chunks.body: Differentiation is part of calculus. It studies how steep a curve is at each point — in other words, how fast the curve is changing there.
chunks.checkText: Differentiation studies...

checkOptions.text: How steep a curve is at each point

chunks.heading: A chord: joining two points
chunks.body: A chord is the straight line segment joining two points on a curve. It's the same idea as a chord of a circle.
chunks.checkText: A chord on a curve is...

checkOptions.text: A line joining two points on the curve
A line touching the curve at only one point

chunks.heading: A secant: a cutting line
chunks.body: A secant is the line through two points on a curve, extended in both directions. It contains the [[mathadv-diff-chord|chord]] joining those points.
chunks.checkText: A secant is a line that...

checkOptions.text: Passes through two points on the curve
Touches the curve at only one point

chunks.heading: A tangent: touching at one point
chunks.body: A tangent is a line that touches a curve at one point and follows the direction the curve is heading there. It shows the curve's steepness at that spot.
chunks.checkText: A tangent to a curve shows...

checkOptions.text: The curve's steepness at one point
The average steepness over the whole curve

chunks.heading: The gradient of a curve
chunks.body: The gradient of a curve at a point is defined as the gradient of the [[mathadv-diff-tangent|tangent]] there. Unlike a straight line, a curve's gradient changes from point to point.
chunks.checkText: The gradient of a curve at a point equals...

checkOptions.text: The gradient of the tangent at that point
The gradient of any chord on the curve
The height of the curve at that point

chunks.heading: The derivative: a new function
chunks.body: The derivative, written f'(x), gives the [[mathadv-diff-gradient-of-curve|gradient of the curve]] at every point x. It is itself a function, with its own graph.
chunks.checkText: The derivative f'(x) of a function tells you...

checkOptions.text: The gradient of the curve at each x
The y-value of the curve at each x

chunks.heading: Sliding a secant toward a tangent
chunks.body: Picture a second point Q sliding along a curve toward a fixed point P. As Q gets closer to P, the [[mathadv-diff-secant|secant]] PQ gets closer to the [[mathadv-diff-tangent|tangent]] at P.
chunks.checkText: As point Q slides closer to P along a curve, the secant PQ...

checkOptions.text: Gets closer to the tangent at P

chunks.heading: The gradient of that secant
chunks.body: For a point x and a nearby point x+h, the secant's gradient is [f(x+h) - f(x)] / h. This fraction is called the difference quotient.
chunks.checkText: The difference quotient [f(x+h) - f(x)] / h calculates...

chunks.heading: What a limit means
chunks.body: A limit describes the value something gets closer and closer to, without needing to actually reach it. Here, we look at what the [[mathadv-diff-difference-quotient|difference quotient]] approaches as h approaches 0.
chunks.checkText: A limit describes...

checkOptions.text: The exact value at one instant only

chunks.heading: The formal definition of the derivative
chunks.body: f'(x) equals the limit, as h approaches 0, of [f(x+h) - f(x)] / h. This turns the sliding-secant idea into one precise formula.
chunks.checkText: The formal definition of the derivative uses...

checkOptions.text: A limit as x approaches infinity

chunks.heading: Using the definition directly
chunks.body: First-principles differentiation means using the [[mathadv-diff-first-principles-definition|limit formula]] directly: simplify the difference quotient algebraically, then let h approach 0.
chunks.checkText: In first-principles differentiation, you simplify the difference quotient before...

checkOptions.text: Taking the limit as h approaches 0

chunks.heading: Differentiating a straight line
chunks.body: For a straight line f(x) = mx + b, the tangent at any point is the line itself. So its derivative is just the constant gradient, f'(x) = m.
chunks.checkText: The derivative of the line f(x) = 5x + 2 is...

chunks.heading: Differentiating a constant
chunks.body: A constant function like f(x) = 7 is a horizontal line, so its tangent is always horizontal. Its derivative is therefore the zero function, f'(x) = 0.
chunks.checkText: The derivative of a constant function is always...

chunks.heading: The power rule
chunks.body: For f(x) = x^n, the derivative is f'(x) = nx^(n-1). In words: take the index as a factor, then reduce the index by 1.
chunks.checkText: Using the power rule, the derivative of x^7 is...

chunks.heading: Differentiating a sum
chunks.body: If a function is a sum of terms, differentiate each term separately, then add the results. So the derivative of g(x) + k(x) is g'(x) + k'(x).
chunks.checkText: To differentiate a sum of two functions, you...

checkOptions.text: Differentiate each term separately, then add

chunks.heading: Differentiating a multiple
chunks.body: A constant multiplying a function stays out front unchanged. So the derivative of a×g(x) is a×g'(x) — just differentiate g(x) and keep the constant.
chunks.checkText: The derivative of 5x^3 is 5 times...

chunks.heading: Expand first, then differentiate
chunks.body: The [[mathadv-power-rule|power rule]] only works term by term. If a function is written as a product like x^3(x - 10), expand it first, then differentiate each term.
chunks.checkText: Before differentiating x(x - 4), it helps to first...

chunks.heading: Another name for the derivative: dy/dx
chunks.body: dy/dx is another notation for the derivative, used when a curve is written as y = f(x). It behaves like a fraction, though it's really a limit.
chunks.checkText: dy/dx is another way of writing...

checkOptions.text: The gradient of a chord only

chunks.heading: Equations of tangents and normals
chunks.body: The tangent at a point has gradient equal to the derivative there. The normal is the line through that same point, perpendicular to the tangent.
chunks.checkText: The normal to a curve at a point is...

checkOptions.text: Perpendicular to the tangent at that point
Parallel to the tangent at that point
The same line as the tangent

chunks.heading: Finding where a tangent is flat
chunks.body: A horizontal tangent has gradient 0. To find where this happens on a curve, differentiate the function and solve f'(x) = 0.

chunks.heading: The second derivative
chunks.body: Differentiating the derivative again gives the second derivative, written f''(x). It's the gradient function of the gradient function.
chunks.checkText: The second derivative f''(x) is found by...

chunks.heading: Negative indices work too
chunks.body: The [[mathadv-power-rule|power rule]] still applies when n is negative. So for f(x) = x^(-4), the derivative is f'(x) = -4x^(-5).
chunks.checkText: The derivative of x^(-2) is...

chunks.heading: Fractional indices work too
chunks.body: The [[mathadv-power-rule|power rule]] also applies when n is a fraction. So for f(x) = x^(1/2), the derivative is f'(x) = (1/2)x^(-1/2).
chunks.checkText: To differentiate the square root of x, first rewrite it as...

chunks.heading: Dividing through before differentiating
chunks.body: If a fraction has a single term on the bottom, split it into separate power terms first. Then differentiate each piece using the [[mathadv-power-rule|power rule]].
chunks.checkText: Before differentiating y = (x^3 + x) / x, it helps to first...

checkOptions.text: Divide each term on top by x

chunks.heading: Functions inside functions
chunks.body: A composite function is built by feeding the output of one function into another, like a chain. For y = sqrt(25 - x^2), let u = 25 - x^2, then y = sqrt(u).
chunks.checkText: A composite function is formed by...

checkOptions.text: Feeding one function's output into another

chunks.heading: The chain rule
chunks.body: For a [[mathadv-diff-composite-function|composite function]] where y depends on u, and u depends on x, the chain rule says dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.
chunks.checkText: The chain rule is used to differentiate...

chunks.heading: Shortcut for powers of a linear function
chunks.body: For y = (ax + b)^n, the [[mathadv-chain-rule|chain rule]] simplifies to dy/dx = an(ax + b)^(n-1). This saves writing out u and du/dx every time.
chunks.checkText: Using the shortcut, the derivative of (3x + 4)^5 is...

chunks.heading: The product rule
chunks.body: For y = u × v, where u and v are both functions of x, the product rule says dy/dx = v×(du/dx) + u×(dv/dx).
chunks.checkText: The product rule is used to differentiate a function that is...

chunks.heading: The quotient rule
chunks.body: For y = u/v, where u and v are both functions of x, the quotient rule says dy/dx = [v×(du/dx) - u×(dv/dx)] / v^2.
chunks.checkText: The quotient rule is used to differentiate a function that is...

chunks.heading: Instantaneous rate of change
chunks.body: When a quantity Q changes over time t, its instantaneous rate of change at a moment is the value of the derivative dQ/dt at that moment.
chunks.checkText: The instantaneous rate of change of a quantity is...

checkOptions.text: The value of its derivative at that moment
Its average value over all time

chunks.heading: Average rate of change
chunks.body: The average rate of change between two times is the gradient of the chord joining those two points, worked out as (Q2 - Q1) / (t2 - t1).

chunks.heading: Increasing, decreasing, or stationary
chunks.body: A curve is increasing where f'(x) is positive, decreasing where f'(x) is negative, and stationary where f'(x) equals 0.
chunks.checkText: A curve is decreasing at a point where its derivative is...

chunks.heading: Continuity at a point
chunks.body: A function is continuous at a point if its graph can be drawn through that point without lifting the pencil off the page. Otherwise, there's a break, called a discontinuity.
chunks.checkText: A function is continuous at a point if...

checkOptions.text: The graph has no break there
The graph has a sharp corner there

chunks.heading: Differentiability: continuous and smooth
chunks.body: A function is differentiable at a point if it's [[mathadv-continuity|continuous]] there and has no sharp corner, so a proper tangent can be drawn. If either fails, the derivative doesn't exist there.
